title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
hook: four friends dig through a roof to lower their paralyzed friend to Jesus

segments.voice: Last week ended at Cana, when the wine ran out and Mary said, do whatever he tells you. Did you notice a need nobody had named? Day thirty-six. A new week: healings and encounters.
screen: `DO WHATEVER HE TELLS YOU.` → `WEEK SIX: HEALINGS AND ENCOUNTERS.`

segments.voice: Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake. Word gets around that Jesus is back, staying in a house, and the house fills. Then the doorway fills. Then the street outside the doorway. Mark says there was no room, not even at the door. Now four men come down the street carrying a mat, and on the mat is their friend. He can't walk. He can't get himself anywhere. They get to the crowd and stop. There's no way through. It would be easy to turn around. Maybe tomorrow. Maybe when it's quieter. These four look up. Today: the friends who went through the roof.
screen: `A HOUSE PACKED TO THE DOOR.` → `FOUR MEN CARRYING A MAT.` → `NO WAY THROUGH. THEY LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: So they climb up onto the roof, carrying him. Then they start digging. Mark says they uncovered the roof and broke it open, and let down the mat. Imagine being inside: dust and bits of clay falling on everyone, daylight opening in the ceiling, and a man being lowered into the middle of the sermon. And here's the line to catch. Mark says: when Jesus saw their faith. Their faith. The friends'. We don't hear a word from the man on the mat. It's the four who carried him whose trust Jesus sees. Then Jesus says something nobody expected: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Some scribes sitting there are troubled, reasoning in their hearts: who can forgive sins but God alone? Jesus asks them which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk. And then, so they'll know he has that authority, he turns to the man: "Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house." And he does, in front of everyone, carrying the mat that carried him. The crowd says: we never saw the like. The Church hears two things in this story. One is the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, where forgiveness and healing are asked for together. The other is intercession: carrying someone to God when they can't get there themselves. That's what Catholics are doing when they pray for each other, and when they ask the saints to pray for them.
screen: `UP ONTO THE ROOF.` · `WHEN HE SAW THEIR FAITH.` · `FORGIVEN FIRST, THEN HEALED.` · `CARRYING SOMEONE TO GOD.` · then, large: `ARISE, TAKE UP THY BED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry someone. Settle and breathe. Think of one person who can't get where they need to be right now. Someone sick, or stuck, or too worn out to ask for help. Picture them on the mat. You're one of the four. If you pray, you can carry them to God in your own words, or with a prayer you know. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with care, and ask yourself what one corner of the mat you could lift this week. The bell holds the time.
Through the roof. Four friends who wouldn't take no room for an answer, and a man forgiven and healed. Today's word.
Your line: friends dig through roofs. Today, lift one corner of someone's mat. A message, a meal, a ride, a prayer. Day thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for one another and ask the saints for their prayers, and the Church offers the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, which the Catechism connects with stories like this one.

fork.setup: you and three friends carry a man who can't walk to a house. the crowd blocks the door. what do you do?
options: wait outside until the crowd thins.
climb up and open the roof.

fork.reveal: they go up, open the roof and let him down on his mat. Mark says Jesus saw their faith.

original.note: Greek: a mat or pallet, a poor person's bed. Mark's word for what the friends carried.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus heals a paralyzed man.
what it means: four friends carry him when he can't come himself, and Jesus sees their faith, then forgives and heals him.
what a scholar hears: the Church links this story to the sacraments of healing, where forgiveness and healing belong together.

notes: Douay-Rheims of Mark 2:11 may read 'I say to thee: Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house.' The quotation begins at 'Arise'; confirm wording.
CCC 1421 introduces the sacraments of healing with the healing of the paralytic (Mark 2:1–12); confirm.
Roof construction (beams, branches, packed clay; outside stair) is standard background; confirm.
'We never saw the like' (2:12) is given without quotation marks.
Intercession of the saints is presented as Catholic practice without comparison; confirm phrasing.
